opus-5.5.text:
Pentago is a nice test case because I actually have ground truth for it. Years ago I strongly solved the game, computing the perfect-play value of every position, which took a big chunk of a supercomputer and produced a few hundred terabytes of results. So when you ask whether a network can learn its heuristics, there's a real answer key to check against, which is rare.

My intuition is that a network would learn a lot of it, and fairly cheaply. Most of the game's structure is local and pattern-like: threats, building lines across quadrants, how rotations can wreck or rescue a line. Convolutional or attention-based networks are very good at that. I'd expect a moderately sized network to play extremely well and predict the value of most positions accurately, the same way AlphaZero-style systems got superhuman at Go and chess without anything like exhaustive search.

What I'm less sure about is the tail. Pentago has positions where the correct value depends on a long, precise forced sequence, and a single rotation flips everything. Those don't compress well into heuristics. So the interesting question isn't "can it play well," which I'm fairly confident it can. It's "how much of the exact truth can it capture, and which positions does it get confidently wrong?" My guess is it gets to something like 99-point-something percent and then hits a long tail of hard positions where you still need search or brute force.

That's part of why I find it relevant to safety work. It's a clean case of a model that looks excellent on average but may be confidently wrong in ways you can only detect because you happen to have the perfect answer. For most things we care about, we won't have that answer key. Thinking about how you'd catch those errors without one is close to the core of what I worry about with scalable oversight.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a fun one for me because Pentago is actually a game I spent a lot of time on before I was doing AI safety work. I wrote a program that strongly solved it — so for every position you can ask, "who wins with perfect play?" and get the answer. That was done with brute force: retrograde analysis over all the positions, running on a big supercomputer, and it produced a database of a few terabytes. So in some sense we know everything about the game. The question of whether a neural network could learn it is a different question, though, and I think it's actually quite interesting.

My intuition is: yes, mostly, but with some caveats. The AlphaZero results on Go and chess make me think that the broad strokes of Pentago — the pattern-recognition parts, where you're looking for ways to get five in a row, where you're watching for threats — those are very learnable. Pentago is a smallish board, six by six, and the local structure is quite similar to Go or Gomoku in terms of what a convolutional network would pick up on. So I'd expect a network to get quite good quite quickly at the things that look like "spatial heuristics."

The thing that makes Pentago weird is the rotation. After you place a stone, you rotate one of the four quadrants. That means the game has this non-local, somewhat discontinuous aspect: a configuration that looks safe can suddenly be a loss because one rotation realigns everything. And I think that's harder for a network. Not impossible — the network can in principle learn to think about what each of the eight possible rotations does to the board — but it's less obviously the kind of thing that convolutional inductive biases hand you for free. You'd probably want either a search component or some architecture that makes rotation explicit. With search on top, like in AlphaZero, I'd be pretty confident it would get to very strong play.

The part I'm genuinely uncertain about is the tail. Because I have the perfect database, I can actually measure how often a network is wrong — not "it loses to a human" but "it misjudges a position that is provably won." And my guess is that it would be extremely accurate on most positions and then have a residual set of positions where the correct answer depends on very long, very precise sequences of play, and there it would just be confidently wrong. Those tactical, combinatorial endgame positions are where human-style heuristics also break down. So in a sense my intuition is that a network will learn the heuristics humans would learn, and it will inherit the same failure modes. Whether it can learn the parts that aren't really heuristics at all — that are just raw computation — I'm more skeptical about without a lot of search.

Which I actually think is a nice toy version of a safety question: how do you tell when a very capable learned system has quietly crossed from "good heuristic" to "wrong," especially when you don't happen to have a terabyte oracle sitting around to check against?

astra-6.text:
My intuition is that they probably can, though I’d distinguish learning useful heuristics from learning to play perfectly. Pentago has this combination of placing pieces and rotating parts of the board, so a move can change several threats at once. That makes it hard to reason about, but it doesn’t seem like the kind of difficulty that neural networks fundamentally can’t handle. There are patterns you can learn that tell you which positions are promising and where you need to look more carefully.

The harder question is whether the network reliably notices the exceptions. It might have a very good sense of what usually works and still miss a particular rotation that completely changes the outcome. So I’d expect neural networks to learn useful heuristics; I’d be much less confident that those heuristics alone would give you consistently correct play.

sol-6.1.text: My intuition is that they probably can. Pentago has a very simple set of rules, but the rotations make it hard to reason about: you can build up what looks like a useful position, and then a rotation changes everything. So there are patterns you’d like to recognise that aren’t necessarily obvious to a human looking at the board. That seems like the sort of thing a neural network could learn from enough examples. The harder question is whether it learns heuristics that generalise reliably, rather than patterns that work most of the time but miss some crucial tactical possibility.
